claims: A naturalized citizen in the United States is a foreign national who voluntarily becomes a U.S. citizen after fulfilling legal requirements established by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).
Naturalized citizens hold the same rights, privileges, and responsibilities as native-born citizens.
Naturalized citizens have the right to vote.
Naturalized citizens can hold public office except for President and Vice President.
Naturalized citizens can obtain a U.S. passport.
As of 2024, approximately 26 million naturalized U.S. citizens lived in the United States.
As of 2024, naturalized U.S. citizens made up about 51% of the total foreign-born population.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires applicants to be at least 18 years old at the time of filing.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires applicants to be Lawful Permanent Residents (Green Card holders).
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires five years of continuous residence as an LPR, or three years if married to a U.S. citizen.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires physical presence in the U.S. for at least 30 months out of the five years, or 18 months out of three years for spouses of U.S. citizens.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires demonstrating good moral character for at least five years before applying.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires ability to read, write, and speak basic English.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires passing a U.S. history and government test.
Eligibility for naturalization generally requires taking an oath of allegiance to the United States.
Naturalization applicants file Form N-400, Application for Naturalization, with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
Naturalization applicants undergo fingerprinting and background checks.
Naturalization applicants complete an interview with a USCIS officer.
Naturalization applicants pass the English and civics tests.
Naturalization finalizes with taking the oath of allegiance in a ceremony.
As of October 20, 2025, naturalization applicants must take a new 2025 naturalization civics test.
The 2025 naturalization civics test has 20 questions.
12 correct answers are required to pass the 2025 naturalization civics test.
In August 2025, USCIS announced it would resume neighborhood investigations for naturalization applicants.
Neighborhood investigations may include requesting testimonials from neighbors or employers.
In 2025, USCIS updated good moral character policy directs officers to weigh positive attributes such as community involvement and employment alongside the absence of misconduct.
Noncitizens serving in the U.S. Armed Forces may be exempt from residence and physical presence requirements.
Noncitizens serving in the U.S. Armed Forces during designated periods of conflict may naturalize without being LPRs.
Children under 18 may automatically derive citizenship through their naturalized parents.
Denaturalization revokes a naturalized citizen's citizenship if illegally procured such as by concealing material facts or willful misrepresentation during the process.
Denaturalization is usually handled by federal courts.
Recent Department of Justice guidance has identified denaturalization as an enforcement priority.
